chapters.t: The reader and his two transmitters
p: Al-Kisāʾī: Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Ḥamzah ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Kisāʾī al-Kūfī, the seventh of the seven readers. He was born in Iraq around 120 AH to a family of Persian origin and died in 189 AH. He was called al-Kisāʾī because he entered iḥrām wrapped in a kisāʾ (a cloak). Ḥamzah was his principal teacher in the Quran, and he studied Arabic under al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad in Basra until he became the foremost grammarian of his generation.
Abū al-Ḥārith: al-Layth ibn Khālid al-Baghdādī (d. 240 AH), a close companion of al-Kisāʾī who read the Quran to him directly.

Al-Dūrī: Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Dūrī (150–246 AH), born in al-Dūr near Baghdad. He was blind, was the leading reciter of his time and the first to compile the different readings. He is the same al-Dūrī who transmits from Abū ʿAmr al-Baṣrī.

Way of transmission: the rules below follow the Shāṭibiyyah (Ḥirz al-Amānī of Imām al-Shāṭibī) and are described by comparison with the reading of Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim. Wherever al-Kisāʾī is named alone, both transmitters agree.
Basmalah between two sūrahs: al-Kisāʾī separates every two sūrahs with the basmalah, exactly as Ḥafṣ does.
Basmalah of al-Fātiḥah: he counts the basmalah as the first āyah of Sūrat al-Fātiḥah, like Ḥafṣ.
Māliki: he reads with an alif after the mīm, like Ḥafṣ: مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ.

chapters.t: Madd, qaṣr and the places of sakt
p: Madd muttaṣil and munfaṣil: both are lengthened to the middle measure (tawassuṭ), four ḥarakāt, the same as Ḥafṣ: جَزَاؤُهُمْ, يَا أَيُّهَا, قَالُوا إِنَّا.

No sakt: al-Kisāʾī does not make the short breathless pause that Ḥafṣ makes in four places; he joins them normally: عِوَجًا قَيِّمًا (18:1–2) with the tanwīn pronounced, مِن مَّرْقَدِنَا هَٰذَا (36:52), مَن رَّاقٍ (75:27) with the nūn merged into the rāʾ, and بَل رَّانَ (83:14) with the lām merged into the rāʾ. In رَانَ he also inclines the alif (imālah).

chapters.t: Mīm al-jamʿ and the ḍamm of the hāʾ and mīm before a sākin
p: Before a vowelled letter: the plural mīm is read with sukūn, without ṣilah, as in Ḥafṣ: عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا.
Before a sākin: like all readers he gives the mīm a ḍammah without ṣilah to avoid two sākins meeting: مِنْهُمُ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ, عَلَيْكُمُ الْقِتَالُ.

Hāʾ and mīm both with ḍammah: when the pronoun is هِم, its hāʾ being preceded by a kasrah or a sākin yāʾ, and a sākin follows, al-Kisāʾī reads both the hāʾ and the mīm with ḍammah in waṣl, where Ḥafṣ keeps the kasrah on the hāʾ: عَلَيْهُمُ الذِّلَّةُ, بِهُمُ الْأَسْبَابُ, يُرِيهُمُ اللَّهُ.
In waqf: when he stops on such a mīm he reads as Ḥafṣ does, with kasrah on the hāʾ and sukūn on the mīm: عَلَيْهِمْ.

General rule: the pronoun hāʾ of the third person masculine singular is lengthened with ṣilah (a yāʾ after kasrah, a wāw after ḍammah) of two ḥarakāt when it stands between two vowelled letters, and of four ḥarakāt, as madd munfaṣil, when a hamzah follows: وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِۦ فَصَلَّىٰ, مَالُهُۥ إِذَا. Al-Kisāʾī applies the ṣilah generally, so he differs from Ḥafṣ in the following words.
Fa-alqihi: فَأَلْقِهِۦ إِلَيْهِمْ (27:28) with kasrah and ṣilah; Ḥafṣ reads the hāʾ sākinah.
Wa-yattaqihi: وَيَتَّقِهِۦ فَأُولَٰئِكَ (24:52) with kasrah on the qāf and ṣilah of the hāʾ; Ḥafṣ alone reads the qāf with sukūn and the hāʾ short.
Yarḍahu: يَرْضَهُۥ لَكُمْ (39:7) with ḍammah and ṣilah; Ḥafṣ reads the ḍammah short.
Arjih: أَرْجِهِۦ وَأَخَاهُ (7:111, 26:36) without hamzah, with kasrah and ṣilah; Ḥafṣ reads the hāʾ sākinah.

Two hāʾs with kasrah: وَمَا أَنسَانِيهِ إِلَّا (18:63) and بِمَا عَاهَدَ عَلَيْهِ اللَّهَ (48:10) are read with kasrah on the hāʾ, and in the second the lām of the Name of Allah is therefore thin (tarqīq); Ḥafṣ alone reads both with ḍammah.
Fīhi muhānan: وَيَخْلُدْ فِيهِ مُهَانًا (25:69) is read with a short kasrah, without the ṣilah that Ḥafṣ makes here.

General rule: where a question is repeated in one passage, such as أَإِذَا … أَإِنَّا, al-Kisāʾī reads the first as a question and the second as a statement with a single hamzah, whereas Ḥafṣ reads both as questions: أَإِذَا كُنَّا تُرَابًا إِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ (13:5), أَإِذَا مِتْنَا وَكُنَّا تُرَابًا وَعِظَامًا إِنَّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ (23:82).
The places: al-Raʿd 5, al-Isrāʾ 49 and 98, al-Muʾminūn 82, al-Naml 67, al-Sajdah 10, al-Ṣāffāt 16 and 53, al-Wāqiʿah 47 and al-Nāziʿāt 10–11.
Al-Naml: in 27:67 the second part is a statement with an added nūn: أَإِذَا كُنَّا تُرَابًا وَآبَاؤُنَا إِنَّنَا لَمُخْرَجُونَ.
Al-ʿAnkabūt: here he reads both as questions: أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الْفَاحِشَةَ (29:28) and أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجَالَ (29:29). Ḥafṣ reads the first of them as a statement.
The two hamzahs: in all of these both hamzahs are pronounced fully (taḥqīq).
Two hamzahs in one word: al-Kisāʾī pronounces both hamzahs fully (taḥqīq). So he reads ءَأَعْجَمِيٌّ وَعَرَبِيٌّ (41:44) with two clear hamzahs, where Ḥafṣ eases the second (tashīl).

Added question hamzah: he adds an interrogative hamzah, read with taḥqīq of both, in أَءَامَنتُمْ in al-Aʿrāf, Ṭāhā and al-Shuʿarāʾ, in أَئِنَّ لَنَا لَأَجْرًا and أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجَالَ in al-Aʿrāf, and in أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الْفَاحِشَةَ in al-ʿAnkabūt. Ḥafṣ reads all of these with one hamzah.

Ibdāl of a sākin hamzah: he reads يَاجُوجَ وَمَاجُوجَ (18:94, 21:96) with a plain alif, الذِّيبُ in Sūrat Yūsuf with a yāʾ, and مُوصَدَةٌ (90:20, 104:8) with a wāw. Ḥafṣ reads يَأْجُوجَ وَمَأْجُوجَ, الذِّئْبُ and مُؤْصَدَةٌ.

Naql in the command of asking: when the imperative of saʾala is preceded by wāw or fāʾ, he moves the fatḥah of the hamzah to the sīn and drops the hamzah: وَسَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ, فَسَلُوا أَهْلَ الذِّكْرِ, وَسَلْهُمْ. Ḥafṣ reads وَاسْأَلِ, فَاسْأَلُوا.
Dropping the hamzah of araʾayta: he omits the second hamzah in this verb whenever it begins with the question hamzah: أَرَيْتَ, أَرَيْتُمْ, أَرَيْتَكُمْ, أَفَرَيْتُمْ.
Other words without hamzah: يُضَاهُونَ (9:30) where Ḥafṣ reads يُضَاهِئُونَ, and طَيْفٌ (7:201) where Ḥafṣ reads طَائِفٌ.
Words with an added hamzah: جَبْرَئِيلَ, مِيكَائِيلَ, هُزُؤًا, كُفُؤًا and دَكَّاءَ, where Ḥafṣ reads جِبْرِيلَ, مِيكَالَ, هُزُوًا, كُفُوًا and دَكًّا.
Dāl of qad: merged into eight letters, sīn, dhāl, ḍād, ẓāʾ, zāy, jīm, ṣād and shīn; Ḥafṣ reads all of these with iẓhār: قَد سَّمِعَ, وَلَقَد ذَّرَأْنَا, قَد جَّاءَكُمْ.
Dhāl of idh: merged into five letters, tāʾ, zāy, ṣād, dāl and sīn: إِذ تَّمْشِي, وَإِذ زَّيَّنَ, إِذ دَّخَلُوا. Before jīm only he reads iẓhār: إِذْ جَعَلَ.
Tāʾ al-taʾnīth: the sākin feminine tāʾ of the verb is merged into six letters, sīn, thāʾ, ṣād, zāy, ẓāʾ and jīm: كَذَّبَت ثَّمُودُ, حَصِرَت صُّدُورُهُمْ, نَضِجَت جُّلُودُهُم.
Lām of bal: merged into seven letters, sīn, ṭāʾ, ẓāʾ, ḍād, zāy, nūn and tāʾ: بَل سَّوَّلَتْ, بَل طَّبَعَ, بَل تُّؤْثِرُونَ.
Lām of hal: merged into three letters, thāʾ, nūn and tāʾ: هَل ثُّوِّبَ, هَل نُّنَبِّئُكُمْ, هَل تَّرَىٰ. When the lām of hal or bal is merged into nūn, the ghunnah is kept: بَل نَّحْنُ.

Bāʾ into fāʾ: a jussive or sākin bāʾ is merged into a following fāʾ in five places: أَوْ يَغْلِب فَّسَوْفَ (al-Nisāʾ), وَإِن تَعْجَب فَّعَجَبٌ (al-Raʿd), قَالَ اذْهَب فَّمَن تَبِعَكَ (al-Isrāʾ), فَاذْهَب فَّإِنَّ لَكَ (Ṭāhā) and وَمَن لَّمْ يَتُب فَّأُولَٰئِكَ (al-Ḥujurāt).
Fāʾ into bāʾ: in one place, إِن يَشَأْ يَخْسِف بِّهُمُ الْأَرْضَ (Sabaʾ 9).
Bāʾ into mīm: ارْكَب مَّعَنَا (Hūd), and وَيُعَذِّب مَّن يَشَاءُ (end of al-Baqarah), which he reads with jazm of the two verbs: فَيَغْفِرْ لِمَن يَشَاءُ وَيُعَذِّب مَّن يَشَاءُ.
Dhāl into tāʾ: عُذتُّ (Ghāfir and al-Dukhān), فَنَبَذتُّهَا (Ṭāhā), and the forms of akhadha and ittakhadha such as اتَّخَذتُّمْ, أَخَذتُّمْ, لَئِنِ اتَّخَذتَّ; Ḥafṣ reads these with iẓhār.
Thāʾ into tāʾ: أُورِثتُّمُوهَا (7:43, 43:72), and every form of labitha, singular or plural: لَبِثتَّ, لَبِثتُّمْ.

Dāl into dhāl and thāʾ: the dāl at the end of the letter ṣād in كهيعص is merged into the dhāl of ذِكْرُ at the opening of Maryam, and the dāl of يُرِدْ into the thāʾ in وَمَن يُرِد ثَّوَابَ (Āl ʿImrān).
Nūn of the opening letters: the nūn is merged into the wāw in يس وَالْقُرْآنِ and ن وَالْقَلَمِ, where Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār.
Abū al-Ḥārith alone: he merges the jussive lām of يَفْعَلْ into the dhāl in وَمَن يَفْعَل ذَّٰلِكَ in its six places (2:231, 3:28, 4:30, 4:114, 25:68, 63:9). Al-Dūrī reads it with iẓhār.

Meaning: imālah is to tilt the fatḥah towards the kasrah and the alif towards the yāʾ. What al-Kisāʾī reads is the major imālah (kubrā, also called iḍjāʿ), midway between the two sounds. Ḥafṣ has it only in مَجْرَاهَا (Hūd), which al-Kisāʾī inclines too.
Dhawāt al-yāʾ: he inclines every final alif that originates in a yāʾ or returns to a yāʾ, in nouns and verbs, when a vowelled letter follows: الْهَوَىٰ, طَغَىٰ, نَادَىٰ.
How to recognise them: put a noun in the dual and a verb in the first person of the past tense; if a yāʾ appears, the alif is inclined: فَتًى gives فَتَيَانِ, and نَادَىٰ gives نَادَيْتُ.

Alif of the feminine: he inclines the alif al-taʾnīth on the patterns faʿlā, fiʿlā and fuʿlā, fuʿālā and faʿālā: التَّقْوَىٰ, إِحْدَى, الدُّنْيَا, كُسَالَىٰ, الْيَتَامَىٰ. The names مُوسَىٰ, عِيسَىٰ and يَحْيَىٰ belong here.

Alif written as yāʾ: every alif drawn as a yāʾ is inclined, including أَنَّىٰ when it asks a question, مَتَىٰ, عَسَىٰ, بَلَىٰ, يَا أَسَفَىٰ, يَا وَيْلَتَىٰ and يَا حَسْرَتَىٰ. Five words are excepted and read with fatḥ: لَدَى, إِلَىٰ, عَلَىٰ, حَتَّىٰ and مَا زَكَىٰ.
Three-letter words from wāw: no imālah in a three-letter word whose alif comes from a wāw: دَعَا, عَفَا, نَجَا, دَنَا, خَلَا, عَلَا, بَدَا, الصَّفَا, شَفَا, سَنَا, عَصَاهُ.
Augmented verbs: once such a verb has more than three letters its alif is treated as a yāʾ and inclined: أَنجَىٰ, ابْتَلَىٰ, زَكَّاهَا.
Nouns from wāw that are inclined: الضُّحَىٰ, ضُحَاهَا, الرِّبَا, الْقُوَىٰ and الْعُلَىٰ.

Individual words: he inclines تُقَاةً (3:28), مُزْجَاةٍ, الْحَوَايَا, إِنَاهُ, كِلَاهُمَا, أَدْرَاكَ and أَدْرَاكُم, تَتْرَا, هَارٍ (9:109), both the rāʾ and the hamzah of رَأَىٰ before a vowelled letter (as in رَآكَ, رَآهُ), and both the nūn and the hamzah of نَأَىٰ.
Opening letters: he inclines the rāʾ of الر and المر, the ḥāʾ of حم, the ṭāʾ and hāʾ of طه, the ṭāʾ of طسم and طس, and the hāʾ and yāʾ of كهيعص.
Verse endings of eleven sūrahs: the final alifs of the verses are inclined in Ṭāhā, al-Najm, al-Maʿārij, al-Qiyāmah, al-Nāziʿāt, ʿAbasa, al-Aʿlā, al-Shams, al-Layl, al-Ḍuḥā and al-ʿAlaq.

Words inclined by al-Kisāʾī and not by Ḥamzah: أَحْيَا when no wāw precedes it, الرُّؤْيَا and رُؤْيَايَ, مَرْضَاتِ, خَطَايَا in all its forms, مَحْيَاهُمْ, حَقَّ تُقَاتِهِ (3:102), وَقَدْ هَدَانِ (al-Anʿām), وَمَنْ عَصَانِي (Ibrāhīm), أَنسَانِيهِ (al-Kahf), آتَانِيَ الْكِتَابَ and وَأَوْصَانِي (Maryam), فَمَا آتَانِ اللَّهُ (al-Naml), and the verse endings دَحَاهَا, تَلَاهَا, طَحَاهَا and سَجَىٰ.
Alif after rāʾ (dhawāt al-rāʾ): a final alif written as yāʾ and preceded by rāʾ is inclined: بُشْرَىٰ, ذِكْرَىٰ, النَّصَارَىٰ.
Alif between two rāʾs: he inclines the alif when the second rāʾ carries a kasrah: الْأَبْرَارِ, الْأَشْرَارِ, دَارَ الْقَرَارِ.

Before a sākin: when the inclined alif is dropped in waṣl because a sākin follows, there is no imālah; it returns when he stops on the word. This covers words with tanwīn such as هُدًى, سُوًى, سُدًى, قُرًى, and words followed by a sākin such as مُوسَى الْكِتَابَ, عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ, رَأَى الشَّمْسَ.

Alif before a final rāʾ with kasrah: al-Dūrī alone inclines every alif followed by a rāʾ that ends the word and carries a kasrah, even when a pronoun is attached after it: النَّارِ, أَبْصَارِهِمْ, حِمَارِكَ, الْقَهَّارِ, مِن دِيَارِهِمْ.

Exceptions: he reads fatḥ, like Ḥafṣ, where a sākin rāʾ merged into the next one separates the alif from the kasrah, as in بِضَارِّهِمْ and مُضَارٍّ, and where the rāʾ is not truly final, as in نَمَارِقُ and فَلَا تُمَارِ.
Al-kāfirīn: he inclines الْكَافِرِينَ and كَافِرِينَ when they are with the yāʾ.

Individual words: al-Dūrī also inclines كَمِشْكَاةٍ, هُدَايَ, مَثْوَايَ, مَحْيَايَ, رُؤْيَاكَ, مَنْ أَنصَارِي إِلَى اللَّهِ, سَارِعُوا, يُسَارِعُونَ, نُسَارِعُ, الْبَارِئُ, بَارِئِكُمْ, آذَانِهِمْ, آذَانِنَا, طُغْيَانِهِمْ, الْجَوَارِ, وَالْجَارِ and جَبَّارِينَ.

chapters.t: Imālah of hāʾ al-taʾnīth and what precedes it in waqf
p: The rule: when al-Kisāʾī stops on the feminine ending, which he pronounces as a hāʾ, he inclines the fatḥah of the letter before it. This is in waqf only, and two approaches are transmitted from him.

The detailed approach, fifteen letters: imālah is made without condition when the letter before the hāʾ is one of the fifteen gathered in the phrase فَجَثَتْ زَيْنَبُ لِذَوْدِ شَمْسٍ (fāʾ, jīm, thāʾ, tāʾ, zāy, yāʾ, nūn, bāʾ, lām, dhāl, wāw, dāl, shīn, mīm, sīn): الْجَنَّة, نُطْفَة, الْقِيَامَة.

The four letters hamzah, kāf, hāʾ and rāʾ: when the letter before the hāʾ is one of these four (gathered in أَكْهَر), imālah is made only if a kasrah or a sākin yāʾ comes before it, and a sākin letter standing between the kasrah and that letter does not prevent it: مِائَة, الْمَلَائِكَة, الْآخِرَة, كَثِيرَة, وِجْهَة, لَعِبْرَة. Without that condition the word is read with fatḥ: سُورَة, مَرَّة, شَجَرَة.
The ten letters: there is no imālah after the ten letters of حَقٌّ ضِغَاطٌ عَصٍ خَظَا (ḥāʾ, qāf, ḍād, ghayn, alif, ṭāʾ, ʿayn, ṣād, khāʾ, ẓāʾ): النَّطِيحَة, السَّاعَة, قَبْضَة.

The general approach: imālah is made after every letter except the alif, so only words like الصَّلَاة and الزَّكَاة are read with fatḥ. Words such as سُورَة, السَّاعَة, مُضْغَة and عَلَقَة are therefore read with fatḥ on the first approach and with imālah on the second.

Ayyuha: in the three places written without alif, أَيُّهَ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ (24:31), يَا أَيُّهَ السَّاحِرُ (al-Zukhruf) and أَيُّهَ الثَّقَلَانِ (al-Raḥmān), al-Kisāʾī stops with an alif: أَيُّهَا. Ḥafṣ stops on the hāʾ.

Feminine tāʾ written open: he stops with hāʾ on every feminine ending written with an open tāʾ, where Ḥafṣ stops with tāʾ: رَحْمَتَ, نِعْمَتَ, امْرَأَتُ, سُنَّتَ, لَعْنَتَ, شَجَرَتَ. The same applies to مَرْضَاتِ, هَيْهَاتَ, اللَّاتَ, ذَاتَ بَهْجَةٍ and وَلَاتَ حِينَ. Where the conditions above are met, this hāʾ is stopped on with imālah.
Sūrat al-Insān: he reads سَلَاسِلًا (76:4) and both قَوَارِيرًا (76:15–16) with tanwīn in waṣl, and stops on each with the alif that replaces the tanwīn. Ḥafṣ reads them without tanwīn.

Definition: the yāʾ al-iḍāfah is the first-person pronoun attached to a noun, verb or particle, as in بَيْتِيَ, ذَرُونِي, إِنِّي. It is not part of the root, it is written in the muṣḥaf, and the readers differ only on reading it with fatḥ or sukūn. The disputed places number 212 and are grouped by what follows the yāʾ.

Before a hamzat al-qaṭʿ: al-Kisāʾī reads the yāʾ with sukūn before an open, broken or rounded hamzah, so the yāʾ is lengthened as madd munfaṣil: إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ. This includes places that Ḥafṣ opens, such as يَدِي إِلَيْكَ (al-Māʾidah) and إِنْ أَجْرِي إِلَّا.

Before the lām of definition: he reads fatḥ, as in رَبِّيَ الَّذِي, and also in عَهْدِيَ الظَّالِمِينَ (al-Baqarah) where Ḥafṣ has sukūn. He reads sukūn in three places: قُل لِّعِبَادِي الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا (Ibrāhīm), يَا عِبَادِي الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا (al-ʿAnkabūt) and يَا عِبَادِي الَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا (al-Zumar).
Before a hamzat al-waṣl without lām: sukūn in all seven places, as in إِنِّي اصْطَفَيْتُكَ.

Before any other letter: he reads fatḥ in مَحْيَايَ (al-Anʿām), مَا لِيَ لَا أَرَى الْهُدْهُدَ (al-Naml) and وَمَا لِيَ لَا أَعْبُدُ (Yā-Sīn), and drops the yāʾ in يَا عِبَادِ لَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْكُمُ (al-Zukhruf) as Ḥafṣ does. Elsewhere he reads sukūn, including words Ḥafṣ opens: بَيْتِي لِلطَّائِفِينَ, وَجْهِي لِلَّهِ, مَعِي صَبْرًا, وَلِي دِينِ.
Definition: these are yāʾs at the ends of words that are left out of the writing of the muṣḥaf; the readers differ on pronouncing or dropping them.

Kept in waṣl only: al-Kisāʾī pronounces the yāʾ when continuing and drops it when stopping in two words: يَوْمَ يَأْتِي لَا تَكَلَّمُ (11:105) and ذَٰلِكَ مَا كُنَّا نَبْغِي (18:64). Ḥafṣ drops both in either state.
Kept in waqf only: he stops with a yāʾ on عَلَىٰ وَادِ النَّمْلِ (27:18) and بِهَادِ الْعُمْيِ (30:53), saying وَادِي and بِهَادِي. In waṣl the yāʾ falls because of the sākin that follows.
Ātāni: he drops the yāʾ in فَمَا آتَانِ اللَّهُ (27:36), the one extra yāʾ that Ḥafṣ keeps.
Ishmām of kasrah with ḍammah: in certain passive verbs al-Kisāʾī blends the kasrah of the first letter with a ḍammah, rounding the lips for ḍammah while sounding the kasrah. Ḥafṣ reads a pure kasrah.

Ishmām of ṣād with zāy: a sākin ṣād followed by dāl is given a share of the sound of zāy, producing a sound like a heavy zāy; Ḥafṣ reads a pure ṣād. The words are أَصْدَقُ (al-Nisāʾ), يَصْدِفُونَ (al-Anʿām), تَصْدِيَةً (al-Anfāl), تَصْدِيقَ (Yūnus and Yūsuf), فَاصْدَعْ (al-Ḥijr), قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ (al-Naḥl) and يُصْدِرَ (al-Qaṣaṣ).

First of two sākins with ḍammah: when two sākins meet between two words and the second word is a verb beginning with hamzat al-waṣl whose third letter has a permanent ḍammah, he gives the first sākin a ḍammah where Ḥafṣ gives it a kasrah: قُلُ ادْعُوا اللَّهَ أَوُ ادْعُوا الرَّحْمَٰنَ, وَقَالَتُ اخْرُجْ, أَنُ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ. This includes the tanwīn, as in مَحْظُورًا انظُرْ, and وَلَقَدُ اسْتُهْزِئَ.
Yaḥsibu: the sīn of the present tense of this verb is read with kasrah: يَحْسِبُ, تَحْسِبُ, يَحْسِبُونَ, يَحْسِبُهُمْ. Ḥafṣ reads fatḥah.
Al-muḥṣināt: he reads الْمُحْصِنَاتِ and مُحْصِنَاتٍ with kasrah on the ṣād, where Ḥafṣ reads fatḥah.
Huwa and hiya: the hāʾ is made sākin after wāw, fāʾ or lām, and in ثُمَّ هْوَ: وَهْوَ, فَهْيَ, لَهْوَ.
Hāʾ al-sakt: he drops the hāʾ in waṣl and keeps it in waqf in لَمْ يَتَسَنَّ وَانظُرْ (2:259) and فَبِهُدَاهُمُ اقْتَدِ قُلْ (6:90). Ḥafṣ keeps it in both states.

Umm: he reads the hamzah with kasrah in فَلِإِمِّهِ الثُّلُثُ and فَلِإِمِّهِ السُّدُسُ (al-Nisāʾ). In waṣl only he also reads kasrah of the hamzah in فِي إِمِّ الْكِتَابِ (al-Zukhruf), فِي إِمِّهَا رَسُولًا (al-Qaṣaṣ), and in the word أُمَّهَاتِكُمْ after بُطُونِ or بُيُوتِ in al-Naḥl, al-Nūr, al-Zumar and al-Najm. When he begins with these words he reads the hamzah with ḍammah like everyone else.
Raʾūf: read short, without a wāw after the hamzah: لَرَؤُفٌ رَحِيمٌ. Ḥafṣ reads لَرَءُوفٌ.
Yā bunayyi: read with kasrah on the yāʾ: يَا بُنَيِّ; Ḥafṣ reads يَا بُنَيَّ.
Kasrah of the first letter: الْبِيُوتَ and بِيُوتًا, عِيُونًا, شِيُوخًا, جِيُوبِهِنَّ and نِسْيًا. Ḥafṣ reads ḍammah in the first four words and نَسْيًا in the last.

Other words read differently from Ḥafṣ: وُلْدًا (Ḥafṣ وَلَدًا), الرِّيحَ in the singular (Ḥafṣ الرِّيَاحَ), يَبْشُرُ (Ḥafṣ يُبَشِّرُ), لَمَسْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ (Ḥafṣ لَامَسْتُمُ), تُمَاسُّوهُنَّ (Ḥafṣ تَمَسُّوهُنَّ), تَسَّاقَطْ (Ḥafṣ تُسَاقِطْ), تَلَقَّفُ (Ḥafṣ تَلْقَفُ), ثَمُودًا with tanwīn (Ḥafṣ ثَمُودَ) and الرُّعُبَ (Ḥafṣ الرُّعْبَ).
